inundate

/in-UN-date/ — rhymes with mandate · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To inundate something is to flood or overwhelm it completely, as with water or an excessive amount of something else.

Fan letters inundated the studio after the finale aired.

Example

After the concert tickets went on sale, thousands of calls per minute inundated the box office, and the phone system completely broke under the load.

The caller volume here is truly overwhelming and literally floods the system — inundate captures both the sense of being swamped and the image of water overwhelming everything, making it more vivid and precise than the plain 'overwhelm.'

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

overwhelm: To overwhelm is to bury or overpower with too much — and it covers feelings as well as floods: grief, gratitude, or homework can all overwhelm you. To inundate needs an actual torrent of arriving things — calls, letters, requests — pouring in like water.

deluge: A deluge is the sudden downpour itself — the burst of rain or the rush of mail that arrives all at once. To inundate describes what that burst does to its target: it swamps them completely, leaving them buried past any hope of keeping up.

swamp: To swamp is the everyday word for being buried in more than you can handle — swamped with chores, swamped at work. To inundate is its formal, more vivid cousin: the same drowning, painted as a flood that submerges everything completely.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

trickle: flow or arrive in a thin, slow stream

drain: draw off liquid until something is empty

Where it sits · how swamped you are by the amount

a few → many → flood → inundate

a few vs. inundate: 'A few' is far weaker than inundate; 'a few' is just a small number, while inundate means being overwhelmed by an enormous amount.

many vs. inundate: 'Many' is weaker than inundate; 'many' is simply a large number, while inundate means so many that you are flooded or swamped.

flood vs. inundate: Flood is close to inundate, but inundate is the more forceful, complete version — to flood or overwhelm something entirely.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — in-: onto, upon (Latin)

Root — -und-: wave; to flow (Latin)

Suffix — -ate: to make, to do (verb-forming) (Latin)

Put it together: In- means 'onto' and -und- means 'wave' or 'flow,' so to inundate is to send waves flowing onto something — to flood or overwhelm it completely.

Use the root in a new word: abundant: The orchard's crop came in so abundant this fall that the family opened a roadside stand.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / neutral

Inundate is a stronger, more vivid choice than 'overwhelm' or 'flood' when you want to emphasize that someone or something is completely submerged in a tidal wave of requests, information, or problems. For everyday situations with mild excess, 'overwhelm' is simpler and more honest.
